name: Kenji Yamamoto
reasoning: Bottom line: I run 8 to 12 meetings a week across three concurrent projects, and the manual work of distributing minutes and chasing down action items probably costs me 90 minutes a day. If an AI notes tool eliminates that, the ROI case writes itself. That said, our clients include financial institutions and public sector orgs — any tool touching meeting audio needs to clear our information security requirements, and that's not a fast process internally. I've killed several promising SaaS trials at the proof-of-concept stage because IT couldn't approve them in time. The other risk: if the summaries require heavy editing to be usable, I've just added a task instead of removing one. I'd want a free trial with real meeting data before committing anything to budget.

name: Masahiro Ito
reasoning: My gemba meetings are fifteen minutes, standing. There is not much to transcribe there. It's the longer meetings — with procurement, with the customer's quality team — where I can see some possible use. But those are also the meetings where a single leaked word can cost us a contract. That tension doesn't go away just because the software has a nice name. I've also watched too many tools get replaced the moment head office switches vendors, and then someone has to re-train everyone. Simple and stable — that's what I need. If the interface is English-only, I won't even bother opening the trial.

name: Yuki Tanabe
reasoning: We run like 8-10 internal and client calls a week and the action items just... disappear into the ether unless I personally chase them down in Slack, which is not scalable. So the value prop is obvious to me — I'm pre-sold on the concept. But here's my actual hesitation: our calls are a mix of Japanese and English, sometimes mid-sentence code-switching, and most tools I've tested just fall apart on that. And the data thing is real — when we're demoing FlowBoard to a prospect, I cannot have some third-party AI storing that conversation on AWS in whatever region. GDPR-adjacent anxiety but for enterprise sales. On pricing, if I have to schedule a 'discovery call' to find out how much it costs, I'm already out — I've wasted enough of my life on that.

name: Rina Ogawa
reasoning: The part of my job that exhausts me most isn't the meetings themselves — it's the hour afterward when I'm retyping my Hobonichi notes into the shared report format. If AI meeting notes software could handle that reliably, I'd genuinely want to explore it. But we handle clients' asset management information in those meetings. There's no scenario where I introduce a tool that records those conversations without our IT compliance team signing off — and if it relies on an overseas cloud server, that conversation probably ends at the first security checklist. What would actually make me take it seriously is if the vendor had already gone through the kind of data residency and security certification process that megabank procurement requires — then I could bring it to the right people with something concrete. Without that, it's a productivity fantasy that I quietly file away.

name: Takeshi Morimoto
reasoning: I've already had to revoke access to two AI tools this fiscal year because consultants signed up independently with their work email addresses — saw a demo on LinkedIn, thought it looked useful, and just… clicked 'sign up.' That's shadow IT, and it's a real problem when the product's terms of service send audio to a US-based server for model training. What would actually make me receptive is a vendor who opens the conversation with their security whitepaper and a copy of their ISO 27001 or SOC 2 Type II certificate — not a feature walkthrough. I'd also want a Japanese-language admin console and a clear per-seat pricing structure with no hidden escalations at renewal; I've been through that before and it's not something I want to explain to the CFO again. Frankly, if a vendor can satisfy those prerequisites, I'm open to running a structured pilot — I'm not trying to block productivity tools, I'm trying to make sure we deploy them responsibly.

name: Ayaka Nishimura
reasoning: On a typical client call, I'm sharing my screen in Figma, nodding along, trying to visually respond to feedback in real time — and also somehow supposed to be writing down decisions? It's genuinely impossible to do both well, and I hate that I always end up reconstructing the meeting from memory afterward. So yeah, naruhodo, this kind of tool is basically made for my situation. But I have three or four clients simultaneously and some of them are pretty protective about their roadmaps, so if the tool is uploading recordings to some server in the US or wherever with vague privacy terms, that's going to be a problem for me to explain to them. Also — and this is a real thing — if the pricing only makes sense at like a team of 20 seats, I'm just not going to bother. I need something that works cleanly for one freelancer, not an enterprise plan I have to beg a procurement team to approve.

name: Sachiko Harada
reasoning: My client meetings involve a lot of personal financial details — income, assets, family situations. The idea of that being recorded and processed by some AI system in a server I can't locate makes me uncomfortable, and frankly it might make my clients uncomfortable too if they found out. On top of that, I'd want to know the interface is in proper Japanese, not some awkward machine-translated screen, and that my oldest staff member — she's been with me nine years and is not great with computers — could actually use it without calling me over every five minutes. If the monthly fee crept up after the first year the way some of these subscriptions do, I'd resent it. But if the time savings were real and I heard about it from someone I trust, not from a salesperson who called during March, I'd genuinely consider it.

name: Shota Kimura
reasoning: The report writing is genuinely the worst part of my day — I'm parked outside a convenience store at 9pm still pecking away at my tablet trying to remember what Dr. Tanaka said in the 8-minute window he gave me. If an AI can listen during the visit and auto-draft something I can clean up in five minutes, that's a game changer for me. But two things make me nervous: first, some doctors would definitely not be comfortable being recorded, and that relationship is everything — I'm not risking a clinic relationship for a productivity tool. Second, if the output doesn't plug into Daiichi Sankyo's internal SFA, I'd still have to manually enter everything anyway, which defeats the whole point. I've already heard some MRs in Tokyo are using tools like this, so I don't want to be left behind, but it has to actually work within our compliance framework.

name: Noboru Watanabe
reasoning: In my thirty-five years of public service, I have seen initiatives rushed into practice without proper foundation, and the resulting corrections have always cost more than the original caution would have. The minutes our division produces go into the official record — if a policy decision is misattributed, or a commitment is omitted, the consequences are not merely inconvenient. Beyond accuracy, I am mindful that our prefecture handles information relating to residents and inter-agency coordination; introducing an AI tool without a full security review conducted through proper channels would be, in my view, an administrative risk we cannot take lightly. The Digital Agency encourages us to modernize, and I do not oppose modernization in principle — but the process matters as much as the outcome.

name: Haruka Fujimoto
reasoning: My actual blocker isn't budget or even the ringi process — it's credibility with skeptics. If I'm going to pilot this at Lion and then scale it, I need a tool that works in our weekly strategy meetings where people speak in keigo, use a lot of abbreviations, and sometimes switch mid-sentence between Japanese and English. I've seen too many 'AI meeting tools' demos that look incredible in a controlled, native-English environment and then fall apart on real Japanese audio. Beyond accuracy, I need the security and compliance story to be airtight — we're a listed company, our meetings contain material non-public information, and if I can't answer the legal team's questions about where data is processed and stored, the whole procurement stalls. The third thing, honestly, is whether the vendor understands how to support a Japanese enterprise rollout — dedicated onboarding, Japanese-language support desk, a customer success person who has actually worked with a Japanese organization before. If those three boxes are checked, I can build the business case and present the ROI myself.
